330.title: Prayer is relationship (CCC 2558–2565)
330.hook: prayer is the raising of mind and heart to God
330.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest says lift up your hearts before the Eucharistic Prayer, and the people answer that they lift them up to the Lord; many Catholics also pray briefly through the day, in short prayers, silence, or the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, carnis resurrectionem: the whole person, body too, raised. Your line was the body too. Today, the last of the Catechism's themes on this path, and the simplest.

Samaria, about the sixth hour, John says: around noon. A woman comes to draw water at Jacob's well. A tired Jewish traveler sitting by it asks her for a drink. She's startled; Jews and Samaritans, John notes, keep apart. Then he turns the whole conversation upside down: if you knew who was asking, you'd be the one asking him, and he'd give you living water. Near the very start of its teaching on prayer, the Catechism comes right here, to this well. Not with a rule. With someone who's thirsty, asking someone else for a drink.
screen: `A WELL AT NOON.` → `A TIRED TRAVELER ASKS FOR A DRINK.` → `YOU'D BE THE ONE ASKING.`

segments.voice: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." The Catechism draws a line from it, following Augustine: God thirsts for us first, so that we might thirst for him. Prayer starts with God's desire. The Catechism gives a classic definition from the monk John Damascene: prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God. Not a technique. A lifting. It adds Thérèse of Lisieux's version: prayer as a movement of the heart, a simple look toward heaven, a cry of gratitude and love in trouble and in joy. The Catechism calls prayer a gift, a covenant and a communion: the living relationship of God's children with their Father, through Christ, in the Spirit. That's why prayer can be words, or silence, or tears, or a glance. Friends don't always talk in full sentences. Right before the great prayer at the heart of the Mass, the priest says lift up your hearts; in Latin, sursum corda. It echoes a line in Lamentations: "Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens." Over these last six weeks you've walked the Catechism: the desire for God, faith and reason, the Trinity, creation, the fall, the Incarnation, grace, the virtues, the Church, the last things. Catholics could say all of it leads here: to a heart, lifted.
screen: `GOD THIRSTS FOR US FIRST.` · `RAISING MIND AND HEART TO GOD.` · `A GIFT, A COVENANT, A COMMUNION.` · `SURSUM CORDA: LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS.` · then, large: `LIFT UP YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Notice what your heart is carrying right now, a worry, a thanks, a person, a tiredness, and hold it without sorting it. Then, on one breath, lift it, the way you'd lift a cup toward someone across a table. If you pray, that lifting is a prayer you can let go to God; if you don't, lift it toward the light, and rest.
Sursum corda, the priest's call before the Eucharistic Prayer, lift up your hearts: prayer as a relationship, a heart raised to God. Today's word.
Your line: lift up your heart. Tomorrow, the last day of year one: the big lookout.
screen: `THE CATECHISM, DAYS 290–330: FROM THE DESIRE FOR GOD TO A HEART LIFTED.`

331.title: The big lookout: year one close
331.hook: stories, practices, the Psalms and Mark, the mystics, the Catechism: a whole landscape seen from here
331.tomorrow: year two opens: a library, not a book
331.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics answer "Thanks be to God" (Deo gratias) after the first readings and at the dismissal, and some parishes sing the Te Deum, an ancient hymn of thanksgiving, on the last day of the calendar year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sursum corda: prayer as a heart raised to God. Your line was lift up your heart. Today, year one's last day.

An hour into the trail, it's all roots and rocks, head down, one switchback after another. You stop noticing how high you've come. Then the trees open: a rail, a bench, and the whole valley below you. The river you crossed at the start, the ridge you thought would never end, the parking lot, tiny now. Three hundred thirty-one days, and a bench at the top of year one. Sit down. Look.
screen: `HEAD DOWN, ONE SWITCHBACK AT A TIME.` → `THE TREES OPEN.` → `A BENCH AT THE TOP OF YEAR ONE.`

segments.voice: Camp one was first words: grace, the sign of the cross, the Mass, Mary, the saints, the rosary, confession, Sunday, the Our Father, Lent, Easter, the Eucharist, mercy, the Psalms. Camp two, the stories: the child, the parables, Holy Week, the cross and the morning, the fire of Pentecost, the saints one by one. Camp three, the practices: the body at prayer, the Mass scene by scene, the rosary, the seven sacraments, confession up close, adoration, the Church's year. Then the text: the Psalms, whose words Jesus cries out from the cross in Mark, then Mark straight through, ending at an empty tomb and a young man saying he goes before you. Then the depths, ways of praying: lectio divina, the examen, the Jesus Prayer, a friar at his pots and pans. Teresa's crystal castle with God at the center. John of the Cross and his dark night. Thomas Merton on a Louisville street corner. Then the Catechism, a map and not a wall, all the way to sursum corda. The Bible has a lookout too. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the whole land at once: Gilead as far as Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, Judah to the far sea, the plain of Jericho, the city of palm trees. The text is honest: he sees it with his eyes, but doesn't cross over. Others will walk it. A lookout isn't the end of the walking. It's where you finally see what you've been walking through. Catholics answer at Mass, after the readings and at the very end: thanks be to God, in Latin Deo gratias.
screen: `FIRST WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `THE PSALMS, THEN MARK STRAIGHT THROUGH.` · `THE MYSTICS, THEN THE CATECHISM.` · `MOSES SEES THE WHOLE LAND FROM NEBO.` · then, large: `DEO GRATIAS.`

segments.voice: Let the year come back, not in order: a word that stuck, a story you told someone, a day you almost skipped and didn't, a day you skipped and came back anyway. Don't grade it; just say thanks for each thing that comes. If you pray, use the old words from the Mass, thanks be to God; if you don't, a plain thank you is enough.
Deo gratias, the people's answer at Mass, thanks be to God: the view from the bench at the end of year one. Today's word.
Your line: you know this country now. Tomorrow the trail goes on: year two opens the Bible itself, in order. See you there.

332.title: Year two opens: a library, not a book
332.hook: the Catholic Bible has 73 books; Protestant Bibles have 66, and Orthodox Bibles a few more
332.howItsDone: Catholic Bibles print seventy-three books, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1 and 2 Maccabees, and the deuterocanonical books are read at Mass through the Church's year like any other part of scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deo gratias: a bench at the top of year one, the whole valley behind you. Your line was you know this country now. Today, year two begins.

Pick up a Bible from a Catholic parish and count the contents page: seventy-three. Borrow one from the Baptist church down the road and count again: sixty-six. An Orthodox friend's runs a few books longer still. Same Genesis at the front. Same Gospels. Same Revelation, or Apocalypse, at the back. And yet the number on the shelf is different. Most people never notice, because nobody counts a contents page. Year two reads the Bible in order, from its first line, so first, a look at the shelf.
screen: `A CATHOLIC BIBLE: SEVENTY-THREE.` → `A PROTESTANT BIBLE: SIXTY-SIX.` → `AN ORTHODOX BIBLE: A FEW MORE.`

segments.voice: Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia: the books. Plural. It's a library, written across many centuries in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, holding poems, laws, letters, family stories, prophecy and prayer. The list has a name: canon. In Greek, kanon was a measuring rod, a straight reed builders used to check a line. It came to mean a rule, and then the list of books the Church receives as scripture, the measure it reads everything else by. The Catholic list has forty-six books in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New: seventy-three. Early councils at Hippo and Carthage, around the year four hundred, gave lists like this, and the Council of Trent defined it in fifteen forty-six. Seven of those Old Testament books, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the two books of Maccabees, plus longer forms of Esther and Daniel, came down to the early Church in Greek. Catholics call them deuterocanonical, the second canon. Protestant churches follow the shorter Hebrew list for the Old Testament; many older Protestant Bibles, the 1611 King James among them, printed those books in a middle section called the Apocrypha. Orthodox churches keep them and a few more, and their lists vary. Each church reads its own shelf faithfully. And why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday: open this library and you're not reading one author's opinion. You're walking into a room where many voices, across many centuries, talk about the same God.
screen: `TA BIBLIA: THE BOOKS, PLURAL.` · `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `FORTY-SIX PLUS TWENTY-SEVEN.` · `MANY VOICES, ONE ROOM.` · then, large: `A LIBRARY, NOT A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Open your Bible to the contents page, or if you don't have one, picture a long shelf. Run your finger down the list slowly, one name at a time, the way you'd read names on a memorial: the ones you know, the ones you've never heard of, and where the shelf changes, from the books of Moses to the histories, the poems, the prophets, then the Gospels and the letters. You don't need to finish; if you pray, ask for a good year of reading.
Canon. From the Greek for a measuring rod. The list of books the Church receives as scripture: for Catholics, seventy-three.
Your line: a library of seventy-three. Tomorrow, the first shelf, and its very first line. Year two, day one.

333.title: In the beginning (Genesis 1:1–5)
333.hook: darkness on the deep, the Spirit over the waters, and let there be light
333.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the first of the Old Testament readings is the creation account from Genesis 1, read in a church lit by candles from the new Easter fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canon: a library of seventy-three books, many voices in one room. Today, the first one comes off the shelf.

It's the night before Easter, and the church is completely dark. People stand in the doorway holding unlit candles. Outside, a fire is struck, a single tall candle is lit from it, and a deacon carries it slowly up the aisle, singing. The flame passes from wick to wick until the whole room glows. Then everyone sits, and the first reading of that long night begins. Of all the pages in the library, the Church reads this one first, in the dark: the opening of Genesis. Bereshit.
screen: `THE EASTER VIGIL, IN THE DARK.` → `ONE CANDLE, THEN A ROOM OF THEM.` → `THE FIRST READING: GENESIS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims, the old Catholic English translation, opens like this: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." In Hebrew, in the beginning is a single word, bereshit, and it gives the whole book its Hebrew name. And the scene isn't tidy at all. The earth is void and empty, darkness is on the face of the deep, and the spirit of God moves over the waters. The Hebrew for spirit, ruach, also means wind and breath. So before anything has a shape, something is already moving over the dark water. Then God speaks, and the line is famous for how short it is: "Be light made. And light was made." A three-word command, and the result in four. No battle, no raw material wrestled into shape. A word, and then light. God sees that the light is good, separates it from the darkness, and calls one day and the other night. Easy to miss: the sun and moon don't appear until the fourth day. Light comes before anything that shines. The Catechism teaches that the world begins in God's wisdom and love, not in accident or struggle. Catholics hear the same opening at Christmas, in the Gospel of John: in the beginning was the Word. And at the Vigil, on the night the Church celebrates the resurrection, the readings go back to the first light.
screen: `BERESHIT: IN THE BEGINNING.` · `SPIRIT, WIND, BREATH OVER THE DEEP.` · `BE LIGHT MADE. AND LIGHT WAS MADE.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · then, large: `LET THERE BE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit for a moment in whatever dimness the room gives you, and notice what the dark does: the edges go soft, the room gets quieter. Then reach for a lamp or a switch, slowly, and watch what appears: colors, faces in photos, the mess on the table, all of it there the whole time. If you pray, say the old line silently, be light made; if not, just notice the difference light makes.
Bereshit, the Bible's first word, and the Hebrew name of Genesis. Before anything, God speaking light into the dark.
Your line: let there be light. Light first, then everything that shines. See you tomorrow.

334.title: Six days and a rest (Genesis 1:6–2:3)
334.hook: the Church reads the days as a teaching about God and order, not a science textbook (CCC 337)
334.howItsDone: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, attending Mass and, as the Church asks, setting aside work that keeps them from worship and rest; the Catechism ties this rest to the seventh day of Genesis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bereshit, in the beginning: dark water, a moving wind, and a single word. Your line was let there be light.

Were the six days of Genesis six real days, twenty-four hours each? People have argued about it at dinner tables for a long time. Some say yes. Some say the days are ages. Some say science and the Bible are simply at war. The Catholic Church's answer steps around the fight. The Catechism says scripture presents the work of creation symbolically, as a succession of six days of divine work, finished by the rest of the seventh. Not a stopwatch. A shape. And the shape ends in something nobody expects from a creation story: a day off.
screen: `SIX REAL DAYS, OR AGES?` → `THE CATECHISM: SYMBOLICALLY.` → `THE SHAPE ENDS IN A DAY OFF.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape. On the first three days, God separates: light from dark, the waters above from the waters below, the sea from the dry land. Rooms are built. On the next three, God fills those rooms: sun, moon and stars for the light, birds and fish for the sky and sea, animals and finally human beings for the land. Separate, then fill. Form, then fullness. Then the refrain. Over and over, God looks and sees that it is good. At the end of the sixth day, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Not just good. Very good. The Catechism, at paragraph three thirty-seven, says the days teach the truth about creation: nothing exists that doesn't owe its existence to God, creation has its own order and goodness, and it is made for worship. The Church holds that faith and science, rightly done, can't contradict each other, because the same God is behind both, and it leaves the science to scientists. Then the surprise. On the seventh day God makes nothing. "He rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." God blesses that day and makes it holy. Not a place, not a person: a day of rest. Catholics keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as their day of rest and worship, and the Catechism links it back to this seventh day.

335.title: In our image (Genesis 1:26–31)
335.hook: male and female, made in God's image and blessed
335.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on human dignity, from the Catechism to the Church's social teaching, starts from Genesis 1:27, and the passage is among the readings couples can choose for a Catholic wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shavat: separate, fill, and a seventh day made holy. Your line was and he rested.

In the ancient Near East, a king could set up a statue of himself in a city he ruled: carved stone, his face, in the square. It said: this place belongs to me, and I rule here, even when I'm far away. A king's image had a job. Hold that picture, and read the end of the sixth day. God has made the sky, the sea, the land, every bird and fish and beast. And then, instead of setting up a statue, God makes a person. These lines are where the Bible says what a human being is.
screen: `A KING'S STATUE IN THE SQUARE.` → `IT SAYS: I RULE HERE.` → `GOD MAKES A PERSON INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Until now, God's commands have run let there be, let the waters, let the earth. Now: "Let us make man to our image and likeness." Jewish readers have explained the plural in several ways, a royal we, or God speaking with the heavenly court. Some Church Fathers heard in it a hint of the Trinity. Either way, the story slows down, as if this one matters differently. Then the line itself, in the Douay-Rheims: "to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them." Both. Not the man in the image and the woman a step behind. The Catechism says man and woman are created with equal dignity, each in their own way an image of God. And what does an image do? Like the king's statue, it stands in for someone. Humans are given the care of the earth, to rule it the way God would, which the Church reads as stewardship, not plunder. The Catechism says this is why every person has the dignity of a person: not something, but someone, capable of knowing and loving God. Last, the blessing. God blesses them, gives them every seed-bearing plant for food, looks at all of it and calls it very good. The Catechism builds on this line; it's at the root of the Church's teaching on the dignity of every human life, from the very small to the very old, the stranger, the prisoner, the person nobody looks at twice. Each one, an image of God set down in the world.

336.title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–17)
336.hook: God shapes the man from dust and breathes into his nostrils
336.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics receive ashes on the forehead, sometimes with words drawn from Genesis 3:19, which tells the man he is dust and will return to dust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, imago Dei: male and female, both in the image, someone and not something. Your line was made like him.

On Ash Wednesday, a line forms down the middle aisle. One by one, a priest or a minister presses a thumb into a bowl of ashes and draws a cross on each forehead. One of the phrases said at that moment comes from Genesis: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. Hours later, some people are buying coffee with the gray smudge still on. It sounds grim. But the story it comes from doesn't start with dust and end there. It starts with dust, and then a breath.
screen: `ASH WEDNESDAY, A LINE OF FOREHEADS.` → `REMEMBER THAT YOU ARE DUST.` → `THEN A BREATH.`

segments.voice: Genesis now tells creation a second time, up close. Not the wide shot of six days, but a potter at a workbench. The Douay-Rheims reads: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Slime of the earth is older English for wet clay or soil. In Hebrew the pun is right on the surface: the man is adam, shaped from the adamah, the ground. An earthling from the earth. Then the breath. God doesn't speak this one into being. God leans in close, face to face, and breathes. So the story makes a human out of two things at once: something as ordinary as the dirt under a garden, and something as close as God's own breath. The Catechism says a human being is one, body and soul together, not a spirit trapped in a shell. The dust matters. Catholics bless bodies, bury them with care, and profess the resurrection of the body. Last, the garden. God plants a garden in Eden, puts the man there to dress it and keep it, and gives one limit: don't eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And that ends a week that started on a lookout, opened a library of seventy-three, saw light before the sun, six days and a rest, an image in the square, and now a handful of clay with God's breath in it.

segments.voice: Take three slow breaths: on the first, notice your body, heavy in the chair, made of the same stuff as the ground; on the second, the air coming in cool and going out warm; on the third, hold both together, dust and breath. Then keep breathing at your own pace. If you pray, give thanks for the next breath before it comes.
Adamah, the ground, in Hebrew: the soil God shapes the first human from, and breathes into, until he becomes a living soul. Today's word.
Your line: dust that breathes. Both halves, the ground and the breath, held together. That's the week.
